title: Charts and Timeframes
lessons/basics-u2-l1/steps/0/body: A **line chart** is the simplest kind of chart: it just connects the **closing price** of each period with a line. It's great for seeing the overall direction, but you can't see each period's high and low.
lessons/basics-u2-l1/steps/1/body: These two charts show all four prices: **open, high, low and close (OHLC)**. On a **bar chart** you get a vertical line from high to low; the tick on the left is the open and the tick on the right is the close. A **candlestick chart** shows the same thing with a colored body.
lessons/basics-u2-l1/steps/2/prompt: Which two charts carry exactly the same information (OHLC) and only look different?
lessons/basics-u2-l1/steps/2/explanation: Bar and candlestick charts both show the open, high, low and close; the colored body just makes candlesticks easier to read. A line chart only has the close.
lessons/basics-u2-l1/steps/3/statement: On a bar chart, the small tick on the right shows the opening price.
lessons/basics-u2-l1/steps/3/explanation: It's the other way around: the left tick is the open and the right tick is the close. Left to right, in the same order as time.
lessons/basics-u2-l1/steps/4/title: Why do most traders use candlesticks?
lessons/basics-u2-l1/steps/4/body: A candlestick chart has the same information as a bar chart, but the **body color** tells you at a glance who won: buyers or sellers. **Candlestick patterns** are read on this chart too.
lessons/basics-u2-l1/steps/4/tip: Plenty of traders switch to a line chart now and then to see the big picture.
lessons/basics-u2-l1/steps/5/prompt: If this were a line chart, what would you see of the highlighted candle?
lessons/basics-u2-l1/steps/5/explanation: The line would only show the close (1.0840). The drop to 1.0800 and the strong comeback by buyers, shown by the long lower wick, would be invisible.
lessons/basics-u2-l1/steps/6/prompt: If you drew this as a line chart, which candle would the line's highest point be on? Tap it.
lessons/basics-u2-l1/steps/6/explanation: A line only connects the closes. The sixth candle has the longest wick but closed low; the highest close (1.0849) belongs to this candle.
lessons/basics-u2-l1/steps/7/pairs/1/mea: A vertical line with two small ticks
lessons/basics-u2-l1/steps/7/pairs/3/mea: The distance from the body to the high or low
lessons/basics-u2-l1/steps/8/sentence: A ___ chart shows only the closes, but a ___ chart shows all four prices with a colored body.
lessons/basics-u2-l1/steps/8/explanation: A line chart is the simplest and only has the close; a candlestick shows the open, high, low and close with a body and wicks.
lessons/basics-u2-l2/title: Timeframes and Picking the Right One
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/0/body: The **timeframe** is how much time each candle covers. On a **1-hour (H1)** chart, each candle shows one hour of price movement, and on a **daily (D1)** chart, each candle is a full day.
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/0/tip: The first letter is the unit of time: M for minutes, H for hours, D for days and W for weeks.
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/1/prompt: The market was open for one full day (24 hours). How many candles does that day have on the 4-hour (H4) chart?
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/1/explanation: 24 hours ÷ 4 hours = 6 candles. On H1 the same day would be 24 candles, and on D1 just one.
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/2/body: A market can be in an **uptrend on the daily** and still fall for a few hours on the **15-minute** chart. That short dip is usually just a **pullback** inside the bigger trend. Lower timeframes show more detail and more **noise**.
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/2/tip: Before you trade, check the higher timeframe so you don't lose sight of the main trend.
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/3/statement: A market can be in an uptrend on the daily and a downtrend on the 15-minute chart at the same time.
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/3/explanation: Each timeframe shows a different window of time. A few hours of falling on the 15-minute chart might be just one small red candle on the daily.
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/4/prompt: EUR/USD is in a strong uptrend on the daily chart. This is today's 15-minute chart. What is this drop most likely?
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/4/options/0/l: A short pullback in the uptrend
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/4/explanation: 12 fifteen-minute candles are only 3 hours. As long as the daily structure is bullish, this drop looks more like a pullback, though nothing in the market is ever certain.
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/5/body: Pick your timeframe based on your **free time**. If you can sit at the charts for a few hours a day, **15-minute to 1-hour** works. If you only have evenings, **4-hour and daily** fit better. Lower timeframes mean faster decisions and more stress.
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/5/example/row: A few hours a day at the charts
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/6/prompt: On the 1-minute chart you saw several conflicting buy and sell signals within one hour. What's the likely reason?
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/6/options/0: Heavy noise on very low timeframes
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/6/options/1: The market was closed that hour
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/6/options/2: The spread dropped to zero that hour
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/6/options/3: Using a line chart instead of candles
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/6/explanation: Very low timeframes are full of small, random moves, and more signals fail. A higher timeframe gives you a calmer picture.
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/7/prompt: Put these timeframes in order from smallest to largest.
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/7/explanation: M is minutes, H is hours, D is days and W is weeks. For example, each D1 candle equals 6 H4 candles or 24 H1 candles.
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/8/sentence: On the ___ chart each candle is one hour, so 24 of these candles make up one full ___.
lessons/basics-u2-l2/steps/8/explanation: H1 means one-hour candles, and 24 hours is one full day: exactly one D1 candle.
lessons/basics-u2-l3/title: Long and Short: Profit Both Ways
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/0/body: In a **long**, profit = exit price − entry price. In a **short** it's the reverse: profit = entry price − exit price. So in a short, the **lower** the price goes, the more you make, and if it rises, you lose.
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/1/prompt: You shorted 1 Bitcoin at $62,000, the price went up, and you closed at $63,500. What's the result?
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/1/explanation: In a short, profit = entry − exit = 62,000 − 63,500 = −$1,500. The price moved against you, so it's a loss.
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/2/title: Stop loss and take profit in a short
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/2/body: In a long, the stop loss goes **below** the entry and the take profit goes **above** it. In a short it's exactly the opposite: **stop loss above the entry** and **take profit below the entry**.
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/2/tip: A short opens at the Bid and closes at the Ask: exactly the opposite of a long.
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/3/statement: In a short trade, the stop loss goes below the entry price.
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/3/explanation: A short loses money when the price rises, so the stop loss has to sit above the entry price.
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/4/prompt: The trend is down, and the price hit resistance and got rejected. Which trade makes more sense?
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/4/explanation: The highs keep getting lower, and the last candle bounced off the 62,300 resistance with a long upper wick. A short with the trend has better odds of working (not a guarantee), with the stop loss above resistance.
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/5/prompt: Which kind of trade do these three lines belong to?
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/5/explanation: Stop loss above the entry and take profit below it, so the profit comes from the price falling. That setup is a short.
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/6/body: In forex, CFDs and **futures**, going short is just one click. But in **spot crypto** you can only sell what you own. Remember, price has no ceiling, so a short without a stop loss **can turn into a huge loss**.
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/6/tip: Never open a short without a stop loss.
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/7/prompt: Your exchange account only has the spot market, and you don't own any Ethereum. You think its price will drop. Can you short it?
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/7/options/0: No; shorting needs futures or margin
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/7/options/1: Yes; just buy Ethereum on spot
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/7/options/2: Yes; with a buy limit below the price
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/7/options/3: Yes; spot has a short button too
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/7/explanation: On spot you can only sell an asset you own. To profit from a price drop, you either borrow the asset (margin) or sell a futures contract.
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/8/prompt: Put the steps of a short trade in order, from start to finish.
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/8/items/0: Spot a downtrend or expect a drop
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/8/items/1: Set a stop loss above and take profit below
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/8/items/3: Close the trade by buying back cheaper
lessons/basics-u2-l3/steps/8/explanation: Analysis first, then your risk plan, then the entry. A short is closed by buying back, and your profit is the gap between the sell and buy price.
